newsitem.title: HUNGARY: RICHTER SAYS COST CONTROL, STRONG SALES BEAR FRUIT.
newsitem.headline: RICHTER SAYS COST CONTROL, STRONG SALES BEAR FRUIT.

text.p: Nine-month figures from Hungarian pharmaceutical company Richter Gedeon Rt are in line with company projections and reflect strict cost control and good sales, the company's CEO said.
"The results don't show anything extra compared to what we forecast in the first half of the year," Richter's CEO Erik Bogsch told a news conference on Thursday.
The IAS results, published earlier today, showed an almost 60 percent rise in operating profits compared to the same period of 1995.
On the Budapest Stock Exchange Richter shares opened higher on the news at 8,450 forints, compared to Wednesday's close of 8,370 forints.
Three-quarter operating profits soared to 7.036 billion forints from 4.41 billion, while net profit jumped to 9.023 billion forints from 6.28 billion forints.
The figures also showed an increase in total sales to 26.608 billion forints from 19.67 billion forints in the same nine months of 1995.
"The figures are the result of strict cost control and good sales work," Bogsch said. "In dollar terms our sales to all (export) areas increased."
A 34.8 percent increase in domestic revenue to 8.555 billion forints was driven by the growth in sales of newer products, primarily Ednyt and Quamatel, he said.
"It's important in the life of all pharmaceuticals companies to renew its product range and I think the recent developments justify this...," Bogsch said.
Last month Richter launched a new drug of its own, Curiosin, for treating leg ulcers, bed sores and wounds.
Bogsch said the marketing of products under licence was also part of Richter's strategy.

At the end of the third quarter Richter launched the over-the-counter sale of Strepsils, a treatment for sore throat, by the licence of Britain's Boots Pharmaceuticals Ltd, Richter said in its result report.
Also in the third quarter Richter signed a licence agreement with Japan's Takeda to market the anti-ulcer treatment Lansoprazole from the first half of 1997.
The former Soviet Union (excluding the Baltic states), which accounted for 42 percent of total export sales of 18.053 billion forints, will continue to be a key market, Bogsch said.

"The strong distribution network continues to be a positive contributor to the company's market presence and whilst the general political and economic conditions remain uncertain, trading conditions remain stable," Richter said in its report.
